entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), established in 1947, was a landmark multilateral treaty aimed at promoting international trade by reducing tariffs and other trade barriers. Originating from the aftermath of World War II, GATT represented a collective effort by 23 nations, including the United States, the United Kingdom, and Canada, to foster economic cooperation and stability in a war-torn world. Its creation was heavily influenced by the desire to avoid the protectionist policies that had exacerbated the Great Depression and contributed to global conflict. GATT is pivotal in shaping the modern international trading system, setting the stage for the eventual establishment of the World Trade Organization (WTO) in 1995.

The initial round of negotiations, known as the Geneva Round, resulted in the reduction of trade barriers and established a framework for subsequent negotiations. GATT's principles emphasized non-discrimination, transparency, and reciprocity, which were crucial in facilitating trade liberalization. Over the years, several rounds of negotiations, including the Kennedy Round (1964-1967) and the Uruguay Round (1986-1994), expanded its scope to include agriculture, textiles, and services, reflecting the evolving dynamics of global trade. By the time GATT was superseded by the WTO, it had grown to encompass 123 member countries, significantly altering the landscape of international commerce.
